title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
hook: Lakshmi rises from the churned ocean holding a garland, and looks over every suitor before she chooses
carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
tomorrow: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters

segments.voice: Yesterday, in this run of Durga and the other goddesses, Lakshmi left the worlds after a garland hit the dirt, and everything went dim. What garland did you pick back up? Day one thousand seventy-six.

The worlds are dim, and the gods are losing. So they do something desperate. They make a truce with their enemies, the demons, and together they churn the ocean of milk, using a mountain as the churning stick and a great serpent as the rope, pulling back and forth like a cosmic tug of war. Strange things come up out of the foam. And then, standing on a lotus, holding a lotus, radiant, the goddess herself rises from the waves. Every god and every demon on that shore wants her. Today, Lakshmi comes back, and gets to choose.
screen: `GODS AND DEMONS CHURN THE OCEAN.` → `STRANGE THINGS COME UP.` → `LAKSHMI RISES ON A LOTUS.`

segments.voice: In the Vishnu Purana, the moment is pure celebration. The rivers come to bathe her, the ocean gives her a garland of unfading flowers, and the gods sing her praises. Then she goes straight to Vishnu and rests on his chest, and the worlds brighten again. But the Bhagavata Purana slows that moment down, and gives Lakshmi something wonderful: a long look. She stands there holding a garland, and she walks along the line of suitors, studying them. In the Bhagavata's telling, she finds something missing in each. One has great austerity but hasn't conquered anger. One has knowledge but can't let go of attachment. One is mighty but can't master desire. One is generous, another is devoted to duty, and still, each falls short somewhere. Then she comes to Vishnu, the one who isn't reaching for her at all, and she places the garland on him. That's the character in one scene. Lakshmi is not a prize handed over to the winner. Nobody wins her by pulling hardest on the rope. She looks, she weighs, and she chooses. And having chosen, tradition says she stays at his side, and goes with him when he comes into the world: some tell of her as Sita beside Rama, and as Rukmini beside Krishna. So yesterday, she left where she wasn't honored. Today, she chooses where she will stay. Put the two stories together, and Lakshmi stops looking like luck that just happens. She looks like someone with judgment, and fortune follows her choices.
screen: `THE OCEAN GIVES HER A GARLAND.` · `SHE STUDIES EVERY SUITOR.` · `EACH FALLS SHORT SOMEWHERE.` · then, large: `SHE LOOKS, SHE WEIGHS, SHE CHOOSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: a slow choosing. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one choice in front of you right now, small or large. Don't decide yet. Just look at it the way Lakshmi looked down the line: slowly, one option at a time, noticing what each one is missing, without rushing to grab the loudest one. Then let it rest. Some choices come clear only after a long look. If you pray, you can ask for good judgment in your own words. If you don't, just keep looking. The bell holds the time.
Durga. The name this run of five goddesses sits under; today it belongs to Lakshmi, rising from the ocean, garland in hand. Today's word.

Your line: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters. Today, before one choice, take a long look down the line before you place the garland. Tomorrow, Saraswati, who began as a river. Day one thousand seventy-six.

howItsDone: Lakshmi is shown seated or standing on a lotus, often beside Vishnu, and Hindus honor her at home and in temples, especially on the night of Lakshmi puja at Diwali.

original.note: Sanskrit: Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune and prosperity, also called Shri; she rises from the churned ocean on a lotus.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lakshmi is luck, and luck just happens.
what it means: in the stories she leaves where she isn't honored and chooses where she'll stay.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 8.8, where Shri weighs the suitors' faults before garlanding Vishnu; the Vishnu Purana tells the moment more briefly.

sources.ref: Vishnu Purana 1.9 (the churning; Shri rises and goes to Vishnu)
Bhagavata Purana 8.8 (Lakshmi considers the suitors and garlands Vishnu)

notes: Bhagavata 8.8 paraphrased: the list of suitors' shortcomings (austerity without conquering anger, knowledge without detachment, might without mastering desire, etc.) is condensed; confirm the examples match the text.
'The one who isn't reaching for her at all' reflects the Bhagavata's point that Vishnu is free of desire for her; confirm.
Vishnu Purana 1.9: rivers bathe her, the ocean gives a garland of unfading flowers, she goes to Vishnu's chest. Confirm details.
Lakshmi as Sita and Rukmini: attributed to 'tradition says / some tell'; this appears in Vishnu Purana 1.9 at the end. Confirm.
The churning itself was taught earlier on the path; here it's compressed into the hook to focus on her choice.
